strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: the paper identifies a genuine gap — no logarithmic-regret results existed for KL-regularized game-theoretic learning with unknown payoffs/transitions (bandit feedback), while such results exist for single-agent settings.

The key technical insight is well identified and explained: best responses to a fixed opponent policy admit Gibbs-type closed forms even though NE policies do not, allowing a 'bandits/RL view' of each player and enabling squared-bonus (rather than linear-bonus) regret bounds. Section 4 gives an honest and informative proof overview including the technical challenges (e.g., unbounded value functions due to positive KL terms).

The proposed 'superoptimism' mechanism (bonuses of the form b_sup = b + 2b_mse plus enlarged projection ceilings) is a novel and plausible device to make the superoptimistic gap property (eq. 30/75) hold, and it is carefully motivated (the H^2 projection ceiling and the factor 3 are explicitly traced to the analysis).

The results are comprehensive: both a regularization-dependent logarithmic bound and a regularization-independent Õ(√T) bound that hold simultaneously, for matrix games (Thm 2.1) and linear-MDP Markov games (Thm 3.1), plus a tighter unregularized bound (App. C.6) and a clean reduction to single-agent bandits/RL recovering the known logarithmic rates.

Detailed and largely self-contained appendix proofs (~35 pages) building on standard tools (confidence ellipsoids, elliptical potential lemma, covering-number arguments), and a results comparison table (Table 1) that positions the contribution accurately relative to prior work.
weaknesses: Purely theoretical contribution with no empirical validation whatsoever. Even simple matrix-game simulations comparing OMG/VMG/O'Donoghue-style baselines would substantially strengthen the practical relevance of the claimed sample-efficiency gains, particularly the dependence on β.

The regularization-dependent bound in the Markov setting is very loose: Õ(β^{-1}d^3 H^7 log^2(T/δ)) versus the single-agent counterpart Õ(β^{-1}d^3 H^5 log^2(T)) and the unregularized Õ(d^3 H^4/ε^2). The H^7 dependence and the quadratic (H−h+1)^2 value ceiling required by superoptimism suggest the analysis is not tight, and no lower bounds are provided to certify that logarithmic regret in T (or the stated H, d dependences) is the right benchmark.

The headline claim of 'logarithmic regret' is somewhat qualified: the log(T) bound is only useful when β^{-1}d^2 log^2(T/δ) < d√T, so the improvement vanishes for small β or modest d; the algorithmic guarantee is really the min of two bounds, and no guidance is given on when the regularized regime genuinely helps in practice (e.g., how β interacts with σ, d, H).

Several supporting proofs are quite compressed and rely on 'follows the same steps as Lemma X' arguments (e.g., Lemmas C.12–C.18), and the main text contains a number of typos and small slips (e.g., eq. (44) derivative computation is hard to parse, 'E3 ∩ E3' on p. 27, 'Incentivize' vs. 'Incentivize without bonus' citation inconsistencies), which slightly reduce confidence in the fine-grained constants, though the overall proof architecture appears sound.

Computational aspects are under-addressed: each iteration requires solving a KL-regularized NE exactly (linearity of the best response aside) and computing three Bellman regressions; only a brief remark cites extragradient linear convergence, with no discussion of total computational complexity.

Limitations are discussed only via future-work directions (instance-dependent bounds, offline setting, general multi-agent/CCE objectives); the strong reliance on the linear-MDP/linear-payoff realizability assumptions and exact known reference policies is not explicitly flagged as a limitation relative to the LLM-alignment motivating applications.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: whether KL regularization yields provable sample-efficiency gains in game-theoretic (not just single-agent) settings, motivated by self-play methods in LLM alignment. The paper is, to my knowledge, indeed the first to establish logarithmic regret for KL-regularized zero-sum matrix and Markov games with bandit feedback, closing a gap left open by prior game-theoretic analyses (Yang et al. 2025a, Ye et al. 2024) that retain O(sqrt(T)) regret.

The key algorithmic ideas are genuinely novel in this context: exploiting the closed-form Gibbs form of the best response to a fixed opponent policy ('best-response sampling'), and the 'superoptimistic bonus' construction that maintains both optimism and a gap property (eq. 30) needed to convert the strongly-concave/convex regularized payoff structure into squared-bonus regret bounds.

The main theorem provides two guarantees simultaneously: a regularization-independent O~(d sqrt(T)) (matrix) / O~(d^{3/2} H^2 sqrt(T)) (Markov, Appendix C.6) bound matching prior unregularized rates, plus a logarithmic regularization-dependent bound. This ensures no regression over existing methods.

The proofs are complete and detailed (Appendices A-C, ~35 pages), built on standard tools (confidence ellipsoids, elliptical potentials, covering arguments) with the genuinely new machinery isolated and explained in Section 4. The proof overview is honest about where the technical challenges lie (unboundedness of KL-regularized value functions, absence of closed-form NE policies).
Related work is comprehensive and the positioning against Zhao et al. 2025a/b, Tiapkin et al. 2024, and Yang et al. 2025a is accurate and fair.
weaknesses: The headline Markov-game result has severe polynomial overheads that undercut its practical meaning. The regularization-dependent bound O(beta^{-1} d^3 H^7 log^2(T/delta)) only improves on the accompanying O(d^{3/2} H^2 sqrt(T)) bound when T >~ beta^{-2} d^3 H^{10} — an astronomically large threshold for any realistic H, d, or beta. Thus in the Markov setting the logarithmic guarantee is essentially vacuous relative to existing sqrt(T) results; only the matrix-game result (crossover at T >~ beta^{-2} d^2) is plausibly meaningful. The paper offers no lower bounds suggesting the H^7 (vs. H^2) blow-up is inherent, and the H^2 factor in the bonus comes directly from the ad hoc choice of a 3(H-h+1)^2 projection ceiling — the gap between regularized and unregularized dependence is left unexplained.

Computational feasibility is a serious concern that is under-addressed. Each iteration requires (i) solving KL-regularized matrix games exactly at every state and stage of a possibly infinite state space S, and (ii) evaluating closed-form best responses (eqs. 14-15) that involve expectations over the transition kernel — operations that are not implementable in the stated generality (S may be infinite). The 'computational benefit' paragraph (linear convergence of extragradient for the inner games) does not address the per-state, per-episode cost or the fact that Algorithm 2 maintains value functions over all of S. No experiments or even small-scale numerical validation of either algorithm are provided.

The superoptimism mechanism appears somewhat blunt: adding b_sup = b + 2 b_mse and inflating the projection ceiling to 3(H-h+1)^2 costs a factor of H^2 in the bonus scale (eta_2 = c2 d H^2 sqrt(log)), which propagates into the H^7 dependence. A sharper design or a demonstration that this is necessary would substantially strengthen the contribution.

The practical interpretation of the setting is questionable: for alignment self-play, one would expect the regularized NE (QRE) to be the object of interest, and the regularized 'exploitability' measured here is w.r.t. the regularized payoff — but the bound's dependence on beta^{-1} means the guarantee degrades exactly where regularization is strong, which is the opposite of the empirical intuition that stronger priors help more. The paper does not analyze dependence on the reference policies (acknowledged only as future work), which limits interpretability of the result.

Writing quality is uneven: numerous grammatical errors ('the originally payoff landscape', 'with with', 'a the same projection operator', 'assume it is true ... assume'), hedged footnoted claims ('could potentially shave off'), and dense notation that occasionally obscures the argument (e.g., heavy overloading of mu, nu, and the sigma^2-dependent term inside O() in Theorem 2.1 is stated inconsistently across the main text and Appendix B).

No instance-dependent or gap-dependent analysis, and no comparison of the achieved rates against what a lower bound might require; the contribution is therefore best understood as a proof-of-concept that log regret is achievable, rather than a sharp characterization.

strengths: Addresses a clear and well-motivated open problem: no prior work establishes logarithmic regret (or linear-in-1/ε sample complexity) for KL-regularized zero-sum games under bandit feedback; prior game-theoretic analyses (Ye et al. 2024, Yang et al. 2025a) only retain the O(√T) rate, while logarithmic regret existed only for single-agent settings (Tiapkin et al. 2024, Zhao et al. 2025b).

The core technical ideas are genuinely novel and well-conceived: (i) best-response sampling exploits the Gibbs closed form of the best response to a fixed opponent, sidestepping the absence of closed-form NE policies that blocks CCE-based approaches; and (ii) the 'superoptimistic bonus' (b_sup = b + 2b_mse) with a raised projection ceiling enforces a 'superoptimistic gap' (Lemma C.4 / eq. 30) that is needed to control the T6-type term and handle the unbounded KL terms in the value functions (eqs. 27–28).

The paper is honest about the technical obstacles — unbounded KL-induced value functions, the lack of Gibbs structure for NE, and why single-agent analyses do not carry over directly — and the proof overview (Section 4) is pedagogically clear.

Results are presented both as regularization-dependent (logarithmic) and regularization-independent (Õ(√T)) guarantees, so the algorithms are no worse than unregularized baselines and degrade gracefully as β → 0; the reduction to single-agent bandits/RL recovers and slightly improves known bounds (β⁻¹d³H⁵ vs. β⁻¹H⁵d³).

The appendix contains what appears to be a complete, self-contained proof development (~35 pages), including concentration lemmas adapted to the regularized value function class (Lemma C.10 covering-number result), and Table 1 gives a careful, like-for-like comparison with prior work.
weaknesses: The dimension/horizon dependence of the headline results is very loose: SOMG's regularization-dependent regret is O(β⁻¹d³H⁷ log²(T/δ)), versus O(β⁻¹H⁵d³) for the single-agent analogue it adapts (Zhao et al. 2025b), and the regularized sample complexity β⁻¹d³H⁷/ε is worse in H than the unregularized Õ(d³H⁴/ε²). The claimed practical advantage therefore only materializes in the very-small-ε regime; no lower bounds are provided to indicate whether the H⁷/d³ dependence (or even the log²T) is inherent, so it is unclear how far the result is from tight.

Several proof steps are only sketched or delegated: T3+T4, T7+T8 are 'bounded similarly'; constants c1–c4 are 'universal' but not specified (one is set by 'choosing a large enough c2 > c′', which is mildly circular); some inequalities (e.g., eqs. 51/53 covariance bounds, the induction in Lemma C.4) involve nontrivial sign/monotonicity arguments (Cov(X, X²) ≥ 0 for nonneg X, policy-swapping lower bounds) that warrant independent verification. I did not find a fatal error, but full confidence requires a line-by-line check.

No empirical validation at all — even a small synthetic matrix/Markov-game experiment comparing OMG/SOMG to VMG or unregularized UCB-style baselines would substantiate that the logarithmic bound reflects actual behavior rather than an artifact of pessimistic constants; purely theoretical results are acceptable at ICML, but the gap-dependent and reference-policy-dependent structure the authors defer to future work limits immediate practical guidance (e.g., how to choose β).

Presentation issues: several typos and small inconsistencies (e.g., 'under the event E3 ∩ E3' should be E2 ∩ E3 in eq. (59); δ ∈ [0,1] should be (0,1) in Theorems 2.1/3.1; Assumption 2 bounds ‖ω⋆‖ ≤ √d which is nonstandard/restrictive; V̄ notation drops the policy superscripts without always saying so; occasional grammatical errors).

The regret-to-sample-complexity conversion (footnote 1) is only sketched, and the computational cost of solving the KL-regularized stagewise NE exactly at every t and state (via extragradient) is not analyzed in the regret accounting.

strengths: First theoretical result establishing logarithmic regret under KL regularization in game-theoretic settings (zero-sum matrix and Markov games with bandit feedback), extending a line of recent single-agent results (Tiapkin et al. 2024, Zhao et al. 2025b) — a genuine gap identified and closed.

Technically novel mechanisms with clearly articulated proof ideas in Section 4: best-response sampling to recover closed-form Gibbs expressions despite the absence of closed-form NE policies, a 'superoptimistic gap' property achieved via a combination of inflated bonuses and a redesigned projection operator, and new covering-number/stability results for KL-regularized equilibria (Lemma C.13) that may be of independent interest.

The proofs are thorough and detailed (roughly 40 pages of appendices), with concentration events, induction arguments, and supporting lemmas worked out explicitly, which supports reproducibility of the theoretical claims.

Well-organized presentation: clean problem setup, a comparison table against prior work (Table 1), honest discussion of technical challenges, and useful auxiliary results including reduction to the single-agent setting (recovering the best known bound of Zhao et al. 2025b) and a roadmap for general function approximation via eluder dimension.

The min{O˜(√T), O(β⁻¹·log² T)} structure is attractive: it recovers the standard unregularized guarantee when β is small or T is moderate, while achieving logarithmic regret in the regularized regime.
weaknesses: The polynomial dependence in the Markov game result is very loose: Õ(β⁻¹d³H⁷ log²T) for the logarithmic bound and d^{3/2}H³√T for the 'traditional' bound, the latter being worse than the prior dH^{3/2}√T result of Yang et al. (2025a). The authors only note in a footnote that Bernstein-style bonuses could shave some factors, and no lower bounds are provided to gauge optimality of the β⁻¹, d, or H dependences.

No empirical evaluation whatsoever; even a simple synthetic matrix-game or tabular Markov-game experiment illustrating the crossover between the √T and logarithmic regimes would strengthen the practical relevance of the claim.

The guarantees are for the regularized (quantal response) equilibrium, and the results require linear MDP / realizability assumptions plus full-support reference policies (implicit in Lemma C.13); the scope is limited to two-player zero-sum games with extension to CCE/general-sum settings deferred to future work, which narrows applicability relative to the LLM-alignment motivation given in the introduction.

The regret improvement is characterized via a min of two bounds rather than a single adaptive guarantee, and the log(1/min{1,β}) factor from the covering-number argument means the bound degrades for small β exactly where the regularization benefit should be strongest.

Presentation polish issues: several typos and grammatical slips (e.g., 'a the same projection operator', 'the the two Q̄ terms', δ ∈ [0,1] in Theorem 3.1 where (0,1) is intended), and the factor-5 vs tighter β⁻¹ constants in the T1/T2 analysis suggest the constants are not carefully optimized.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: whether KL regularization yields provable sample-efficiency gains in game-theoretic settings, complementing the known computational gains in the full-information setting and the recent logarithmic-regret results in the single-agent setting (Zhao et al., 2025b; Tiapkin et al., 2024).

First (to the authors' knowledge, and plausibly correct) logarithmic regret guarantees for learning the KL-regularized NE in two-player zero-sum matrix and Markov games under bandit feedback, alongside matching regularization-independent √T guarantees in a min{·} form so the algorithm never does worse than standard optimism.

The algorithmic ideas are genuinely interesting: (i) best-response sampling, which restores the closed-form Gibbs structure that is absent for NE policies in games, and (ii) 'superoptimism' (inflated bonuses plus a raised projection ceiling) to obtain a superoptimistic gap property, which is a novel technical device for the game setting.

Section 4 provides a genuinely useful proof overview that identifies the real technical challenges (absence of closed-form NE, unbounded value functions due to positive KL terms, covering-number analysis of the induced superoptimistic value class), and the supporting lemmas (e.g., Lemma C.12 three-point identity, Lemma C.13 payoff-perturbation stability) may be of independent interest.

Extensive, self-contained appendices with complete proofs, and useful discussions of reductions to the single-agent setting (recovering the best known bound of Zhao et al., 2025b) and extensions to general function approximation via eluder dimension.
weaknesses: The bounds are of primarily conceptual value: the logarithmic Markov-game guarantee carries a large H^7 d^3 dependence and the min-player bound inherits log(1/β) and log(1/δ min{1,β}) terms, so the improvement over Õ(√T) only materializes at large T; no instance-dependent or lower-bound analysis is provided to show the β^{-1} (or the poly factors) is at all tight, leaving the practical significance of the result unclear.

The work is purely theoretical with no empirical validation, and the algorithms are computationally expensive: each iteration requires solving a KL-regularized zero-sum matrix game (per state/h for SOMG) to the NE, plus three regressions per level; the claimed extragradient-based subroutine adds substantial overhead that is not analyzed end-to-end.

Several presentation and correctness-adjacent slips undermine confidence: Lemma A.6 states an equality (min{1,·} = ∥xt∥²_{V^{-1}}) where an inequality is meant; the statement 'the penultimate line comes from event E3 ∩ E3' (p. 28) is a typo; Lemma C.13 is invoked in the proof of Lemma C.11 before it is stated; δ is declared in [0,1] (including δ=0); minor typos such as 'Incentivize', inconsistent tabular/pagination issues, and Proposition 3.1's proof being 'contained in' proofs of other lemmas rather than given directly.

The comparison in Table 1 is somewhat asymmetric: the 'Reg.' entries of prior work (Yang et al., 2025a) and the proposed methods optimize different objectives (regularized NE with β-dependent policies vs. unregularized NE), and the footnote translation of O'Donoghue et al. (2021) from tabular to linear function approximation makes the head-to-head comparison approximate; a cleaner apples-to-apples framing (e.g., regret for the unregularized value under a regularized algorithm) would help.

Key assumptions are strong and standard-but-heavy: linear MDP with signed-measure features and ∥ψh∥, ∥ωh∥ ≤ √d, plus bounded-noise realizability for matrix games; the generality of the contribution beyond these classes is only sketched (Appendix D.2) rather than proven.

Parts of the proofs lean on adapted arguments from Zhao et al. (2025b) and the 'bandits/RL view' reduction; the genuinely new machinery (superoptimism, covering numbers of the superoptimistic class) is sound but the overall novelty over that line of work is incremental rather than a new framework.

No reproducibility support is applicable (no code), and limitations such as the reliance on full-support reference policies (needed for Lemma C.13 and the KL three-point identity) are not explicitly discussed as an assumption with practical consequences for LLM self-play, the paper's motivating application.

strengths: Clear and important gap identified: while logarithmic regret under KL regularization is known for single-agent bandits/RL (Tiapkin et al. 2024, Zhao et al. 2025b), no such result existed for game-theoretic settings; this paper is plausibly the first to close it, for both matrix and Markov games.

Technically novel mechanisms: best-response sampling to recover closed-form Gibbs-style structure absent for NE policies, a 'superoptimistic gap' (Lemma C.4) obtained via enlarged bonuses and a non-standard projection operator (ceiling 3(H−h+1)²) to handle unbounded regularized value functions, and a covering-number argument exploiting KL-induced stability of NE policies under payoff perturbations (Lemma C.13).

Comprehensive and careful appendix: full proofs for both settings (Sections B, C), honest proof overview (Section 4) that explicitly names the technical challenges (absence of closed-form NE, unbounded value functions, covering numbers), and useful auxiliary results (KL three-point identity, stability under payoff perturbations) that may be of independent interest.

The dual bounds are well-designed: a β⁻¹d²log²T (resp. β⁻¹d³H⁷log²T) logarithmic guarantee for β>0 combined with a regularization-independent √T guarantee holds simultaneously, so the algorithm degrades gracefully to the unregularized rate as β→0.

Helpful additional discussions: reduction to the single-agent setting recovers the best known bound of Zhao et al. [2025b], and a roadmap for extending to general function approximation via Eluder-dimension bonuses is provided.
weaknesses: No lower bounds are given, so it is unclear whether the β⁻¹ log²(T) dependence, or the polynomial factors (d³H⁷ in the Markov case), are near-optimal; the paper also does not discuss potential improvements to log(T) rather than log²(T).

The √T fallback bound for Markov games (d^{3/2}H³√T) is worse in d and H than prior work (Yang et al. 2025a: dH^{3/2}√T), so the contribution rests entirely on the logarithmic term; the H⁷ dependence is heavy, and the claimed potential Bernstein-bonus improvement is only a footnote remark, not carried out.

Purely theoretical: no experiments or empirical validation of the algorithms, and the practical computational cost of solving stage-wise KL-regularized NEs at every (t, h) in SOMG is only briefly addressed.

Several presentation and consistency issues: typos (e.g., 'E3 ∩ E3' on p.28, 'penultimate'/'the the'), inconsistent δ ranges ([0,1] vs (0,1)) across theorem statements, minor log-form discrepancies between Theorem 2.1 and its appendix version (Theorem B.1), and informal phrase 'the event E3' instead of 'E2 ∩ E3' in one step of the matrix-game proof.

The analysis leans on supporting arguments imported from Zhao et al. [2025b] (bandits/RL views) plus the new superoptimism machinery; while the assembly is nontrivial, parts of the concentration scaffolding (Lemmas A.2–A.8) are standard, which somewhat tempers the novelty assessment.

Some proof steps are stated at a high level and rely on asserted parallels (e.g., eq. (26) and the T2 bound via Lemma B.1, the 'analogous arguments' for T3–T8), so a careful reader must reconstruct several symmetric cases; assumptions on full support of reference policies (needed for Lemma C.12/C.13) are only stated where used, not consolidated.
